Use the warm up to check pupils’ prior knowledge of aquatic breathing. Pupils play “Breathing Holes.” Hoops or noodles are placed on the surface of the water.
Pupils must go over and under, breathing when they surface.
Front crawl body position and leg action
as a repeated swim with rest intervals helps improve stamina and stroke efficiency as well as preparing us for attendance
push and glide (blast off) - 1 hand on top of the other at the surface of the water, arms extended
leg action - a steady and continuous, alternating flutter kick with relaxed ankles and pointed toes
Being a timekeeper is an excellent way to learn how to use a stopwatch or pace clock and how to work out improvement in performance.
Striving to improve the use of a long, streamlined body position when gliding and aiming to improve our swimming times requires resilience and self-motivation.
stroke for 45 seconds. Have a 10 second rest and repeat.
Pupils work in pairs, 1 pupil being the time keeper, 1 pupil performing the task.

“Blast off” - pupils perform a push and glide from the wall and swim 5m with arms extended (1 hand on top of the other) using only their legs only. The other pupil times how long it takes their partner to complete the swim and provides feedback on performance.
Pupils then repeat the activity to see if they can go faster after receiving feedback from their partner.
Move: pupils can remain in a streamlined position whilst kicking their legs to help increase the speed at which they are travelling.
Feel: pupils always strive to improve their performance, by feeling their body stretch in a long streamlined position showing resilience and self-motivation.

Having a lower stroke count means that the underwater phase of the arm action is efficient and uses less energy. The arm action of the stroke will change depending on the intended purpose, for example, when swimming with a water polo ball the arm action will be wider to keep the ball under control.

The head is turned to the side to maintain a streamlined body position. Lifting the head would result in the legs dropping and slowing you down.
When working with a partner it is really important to provide feedback in a positive and informed manner, showing respect.
Holding a noodle on the surface of the water out in front with a “window” space created for the head, pupils kick across the pool with their faces in the water blowing bubbles for 3 seconds.
Pupils turn their head to the side to clear the face of the water to inhale.
The face returns to the water for 3 seconds and then repeats to the opposite side.

arm action with their faces in the water blowing bubbles, they turn their head to the side every third arm cycle to inhale and return their head to the water.
Working in pairs, one pupil counts for their partner and says “1, 2 breath” whilst their partner swims across the pool
turning their head to the side every third arms cycle to inhale. Feedback is provided and then pupils swap roles.

Pupils perform head first and feet first sculling action. Play a game of “dodgems” where pupils have to avoid each other whilst sculling around a small teaching area with the legs over the noodle like they are sat in a bumper car. When they are near to other pupils they have to use a sculling action to change direction, if they “bump” into another pupil they have to scull 360 degrees in each direction.
